strengths: Compelling motivation and empirical grounding: The paper clearly identifies and visualizes two prominent redundancies in Visual Autoregressive (VAR) models—scale redundancy (attention primarily focuses on the immediately preceding scale) and spatial redundancy (attention between scales is diagonally concentrated around local spatial neighborhoods).

Clean and effective formulation: Introducing scale- and spatial-Markovian conditioning naturally simplifies multi-scale autoregressive modeling. A major practical advantage is the elimination of the KV cache during inference, which significantly lowers peak GPU memory footprint (by up to 3–4x) and enables parallelized training across scales.

Solid quantitative results: On ImageNet 256x256, MVAR improves upon the baseline VAR across standard generative metrics (e.g., FID drops from 3.55 to 3.09 for the 310M model) while substantially decreasing memory usage and computational overhead.

Comprehensive ablation studies: The ablations systematically analyze the effect of varying conditioning history (number of preceding scales) and neighborhood window size k, validating the design choices.
weaknesses: Incomplete scratch training across scales: Only the base 310M model is trained from scratch; the larger models (d20 at 600M and d24 at 1.0B) are only fine-tuned from pre-trained VAR checkpoints. It remains somewhat unclear whether large-scale models trained purely from scratch under the Markovian formulation maintain or extend these gains without pre-training initialization.

Architectural novelty is evolutionary: The concept of neighborhood/local window attention across hierarchical stages is well-established in vision transformers (e.g., NAT, DiNAT). The core contribution lies in porting these locality priors to next-scale autoregressive generation rather than inventing a fundamentally new algorithmic mechanism.

Scope limited to ImageNet 256x256: The empirical validation is restricted to 256x256 resolution. A primary motivation for KV-cache-free and linear-complexity visual modeling is scaling to higher resolutions (e.g., 512x512, 1024x1024) or video generation; demonstrating MVAR on higher resolutions would have significantly strengthened the practical significance of the claims.

strengths: Well-motivated design grounded in empirical observations: The paper effectively visualizes and analyzes attention weights in vanilla VAR, clearly demonstrating the scale redundancy (attention predominantly concentrates on the immediate prior scale) and spatial redundancy (attention is concentrated in localized neighborhoods).

High practical impact and efficiency gains: Restricting attention to adjacent scales and local spatial neighborhoods eliminates the KV cache during autoregressive inference and reduces GPU memory footprint by 3.0x to 4.2x, enabling 1.0B model training/fine-tuning and inference on consumer GPUs (e.g., RTX 4090) without out-of-memory errors.

Strong generative performance: Across ImageNet 256x256 class-conditional benchmarks, MVAR achieves competitive or improved FID and Inception Scores compared to vanilla VAR baselines (e.g., FID drops from 3.55 to 3.09 for the 310M model trained from scratch, and 2.33 to 2.23 for the fine-tuned 1.0B model).

Solid ablations and theoretical analysis: The paper provides clear complexity analyses showing the reduction from O(N^2) to O(Nk), alongside systematic ablation studies on the number of conditioning scales and neighborhood window sizes (k).
weaknesses: Modest wall-clock inference speedup: While memory savings and KV cache elimination are substantial, the actual reduction in wall-clock inference latency is relatively incremental (e.g., 0.81s to 0.71s on VAR-d24), likely due to non-attention overheads and specialized GPU kernel optimization limits for local window attention at 256x256 resolution.

Details on cross-scale coordinate mapping: Because adjacent scales in VAR have different spatial grid dimensions (e.g., 10x10 to 13x13, 13x13 to 16x16), the exact mechanism for locating and interpolating the center and neighborhood of the k-nearest tokens across mismatched resolutions could be detailed more explicitly in Section 3.3.

Evaluation scope: Experiments are restricted to class-conditional ImageNet 256x256. Benchmarking on higher resolutions (512x512) or text-to-image synthesis would have demonstrated the scalability and practical impact of a KV-cache-free autoregressive model even more compellingly.

strengths: Clear empirical motivation: The paper provides convincing analysis and visualizations showing that cross-scale attention in VAR predominantly focuses on the immediately preceding scale and exhibits strong spatial locality.

Practical memory and inference benefits: Reformulating next-scale generation as a first-order Markov process completely eliminates the requirement of maintaining a multi-scale KV cache during inference, resulting in a substantial reduction in GPU memory usage (~3.0x to 4.2x) and enabling training larger models on commodity GPUs (e.g., RTX 4090).

Solid empirical performance: MVAR achieves competitive results on ImageNet 256x256 class-conditional generation, matching or outperforming standard VAR baselines both when trained from scratch (FID 3.09 vs. 3.55) and when fine-tuning existing checkpoints.
Comprehensive ablation studies: The ablations systematically explore the conditioning window length (Markov order) and neighborhood window size k, justifying the chosen design configurations.
weaknesses: Under-specified coordinate alignment across scales: The paper lacks a precise formal definition of how spatial correspondence $\eta_k(r_{l-1})$ is established between adjacent scales $r_l$ and $r_{l-1}$ when their spatial dimensions differ (e.g., progressing from $10\times 10$ to $13\times 13$ and $16\times 16$). Clarifying whether coordinates are mapped via spatial interpolation, fractional nearest neighbors, or ROI pooling is essential for reproducibility.

Limited wall-clock speedup relative to theoretical claims: Although the theoretical complexity is reduced from $O(N^2)$ to $O(Nk)$, the actual reduction in attention GFLOPs (e.g., from 43.61 to 35.44) and inference runtime (0.34s to 0.27s) is relatively modest. This occurs because total sequence length in 256x256 VAR is only 680 tokens, where attention computation is not the dominant wall-clock bottleneck compared to feed-forward network layers.

Ad-hoc handling of causal masking at fine scales: In Appendix A, the authors mention disabling causal masking for scales $r_9$ and $r_{10}$. The theoretical and architectural justification for treating the final two scales differently from scales $r_1$–$r_8$ is insufficiently explained.

Incremental algorithmic novelty: Restricting attention to immediate predecessors (first-order Markov assumption) and applying localized neighborhood attention are relatively direct adaptations of established concepts (e.g., Neighborhood Attention / local windowing) to the multi-scale autoregressive setup.

strengths: The paper is motivated by clear empirical observations: analyzing VAR reveals that attention is predominantly concentrated on the immediately preceding scale and spatially localized within a compact neighborhood.

The proposed scale-Markov and spatial-Markov conditioning effectively eliminate the KV cache requirement during inference, reducing inference GPU memory by approximately 3x and lowering computational complexity from O(N^2) to O(Nk).

Solid empirical performance: MVAR achieves better FID and IS compared to the baseline VAR on ImageNet 256x256 both when trained from scratch (MVAR-d16 FID 3.09 vs. VAR-d16 FID 3.55) and when fine-tuning existing VAR checkpoints.
Comprehensive experimental evaluation and ablations across multiple resolutions (256x256, 512x512), datasets (ImageNet, CelebA, FFHQ), receptive field sizes k, and conditioning prefixes.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is somewhat incremental, as it primarily combines first-order Markovian conditioning across scales with existing neighborhood attention kernels (e.g., Hassani & Shi) within the VAR framework.

The training pipeline is somewhat fragmented: scales r1–r8 are trained concurrently via diagonal attention masks, while scales r9 and r10 are trained separately using custom CUDA kernels in an alternating ratio scheme (mixed training strategy). This adds operational complexity compared to standard autoregressive training.

Due to computational constraints, the larger models (e.g., d24 and the 2B model) and higher-resolution experiments (512x512) are trained under abbreviated schedules (50–100 epochs with small batch sizes), leaving some open questions regarding scalability under full-scale training regimes.

strengths: Compelling motivation and empirical justification: The authors provide intuitive and clear empirical evidence (attention maps and accumulated attention weights) demonstrating that next-scale prediction in VAR is both cross-scale redundant (predominantly relying on the adjacent scale) and spatially localized.

Substantial efficiency gains: By enforcing scale-Markovian and spatial-Markovian assumptions, the model completely removes the requirement for a KV cache during inference and reduces attention complexity from O(N^2) to O(Nk), resulting in a ~3-4x reduction in inference memory and enabling training on consumer-grade hardware (RTX 4090s).

Strong generative performance: Across ImageNet 256x256, MVAR matches or improves upon baseline VAR in both FID and Inception Score (e.g., FID drops from 3.55 to 3.09 for d16 from scratch), demonstrating that restricting attention acts as an effective inductive bias rather than hurting performance.

Comprehensive empirical validation: The paper includes extensive ablations on context scale length, neighborhood size k, training schedules/ratios, as well as evaluations across different resolutions (512x512) and datasets (CelebA, FFHQ).
weaknesses: Incremental methodological novelty: The algorithmic building blocks—namely first-order Markov assumptions along the scale dimension and neighborhood/windowed attention (e.g., Neighborhood Attention Transformer)—are well-established techniques. Their combination in the context of VAR is intuitive and effective, but the conceptual novelty is relatively modest.

Mixed training pipeline complexity: The training scheme is somewhat fragmented, where scales r1-r8 are trained in parallel with causal masks, while the finest scales (r9, r10) require separate training iterations and custom CUDA kernels. While justified by memory constraints, this introduces additional hyperparameter tuning (e.g., the mixed training iteration ratio).

Recall / Diversity degradation: In Table 2, fine-tuned MVAR models consistently exhibit a slight drop in Recall compared to the dense VAR baselines (e.g., 0.51 to 0.48 for d16, 0.56 to 0.52 for d20, and 0.59 to 0.56 for d24), suggesting that strictly local conditioning may slightly restrict mode coverage.

Main ImageNet models beyond 310M are fine-tuned rather than trained from scratch: Due to compute constraints, the larger ImageNet models (d20, d24) are fine-tuned from pretrained VAR weights for 80 epochs rather than trained fully from scratch, leaving some questions about whether full pretraining from scratch scales equally stably for larger architectures on ImageNet.

strengths: Clear empirical motivation: The paper provides insightful analyses of attention maps in vanilla Visual AutoRegressive (VAR) models, demonstrating that attention weights are heavily concentrated on the immediately preceding scale and are spatially localized.

Substantial memory and compute savings: By enforcing a scale-Markov property, MVAR completely removes the need to store inter-scale KV caches during autoregressive inference, achieving a 2.8× to 4.2× reduction in GPU memory footprint.

Solid empirical performance: MVAR achieves competitive or slightly improved FID and Inception Scores compared to VAR on ImageNet 256×256 across multiple model sizes (d16, d20, d24), and exhibits consistent behavior across additional datasets (CelebA, FFHQ) and resolutions (512×512).
Thorough ablations: The ablation studies systematically evaluate the impact of scale history length (number of conditioning prefix scales) and neighborhood window size $k$.
weaknesses: Misleading time complexity analysis: In Section 3.4 and Appendix A (Eq. 9), the authors claim that standard next-token autoregressive generation has a time complexity of $\mathcal{O}(N^3)$, which only holds if attention is recomputed from scratch at every step without a KV cache. With standard KV caching, next-token generation complexity is $\mathcal{O}(N^2)$. Contrasting MVAR with an un-cached $\mathcal{O}(N^3)$ baseline is technically misleading.

Limited conceptual novelty: The core methodological contribution is largely an amalgamation of two well-established techniques—an order-1 Markov chain across resolution scales (a standard assumption in classical multiscale pyramids) and Neighborhood Attention (NAT/DiNAT) applied to cross-scale attention.

Incomplete from-scratch evaluation on larger scales: On ImageNet-1K, only the smallest configuration (d16, 310M) is trained from scratch. The larger models (d20 and d24) are only evaluated by fine-tuning pre-trained VAR checkpoints, leaving it unverified whether large MVAR models can train stably from scratch without relying on dense representations learned by standard VAR.

Ad-hoc training pipeline: Scales $r_1$ through $r_8$ are trained jointly with diagonal causal masking, whereas scales $r_9$ and $r_{10}$ must be decoupled and trained separately via custom CUDA kernels and an interleaved iteration ratio (e.g., 8:1:1), adding noticeable engineering complexity and fragmentation to the training pipeline.

Clarity and formatting defects: There is an empty section heading ('3.1 KEY OBSERVATIONS') immediately preceding '3.2 PRELIMINARY', and prominent citation errors exist in the main text and references (e.g., Brock et al. cited as '1809' instead of '2018').
